prerequisiteEdges.justification: Simplifying is the reverse of generating equivalents, so learners must already see that multiplying or dividing both parts keeps the same amount.
Percent and hundredths forms are recognised as the same rational only after the fraction can be written with a convenient denominator.
Placing a fraction on an unmarked interval requires seeing it as equal to another fraction whose denominator matches the chosen scale.
A ratio written as a fraction of the total parts is meaningful only if equivalent fractions of that whole are already understood.
Sharing requires treating the ratio numbers as parts of a common whole whose size is first found from the total.
Applied mixes often switch among 1:4, 1/5 and 0.2, so those representations must already be interchangeable.
Modelling a recipe or mix is the same partition skill applied to a messy real quantity rather than a tidy whole-number total.

misconceptions.label: Adds numerators and denominators
misconceptions.description: Creates a new fraction by adding the two numerators and adding the two denominators instead of using a common multiple or divisor.

misconceptions.label: Treats ratio parts as unrelated
misconceptions.description: Reads 2:3 as two separate counts with no shared whole, so cannot form the fraction 2/5 or 3/5 of the total.

misconceptions.label: Splits using the written numbers only
misconceptions.description: Gives $2 and $3 when asked to share $20 in the ratio 2:3, ignoring that the parts must first be scaled to the actual total.

misconceptions.label: Drops units when mixing
misconceptions.description: Applies the ratio numbers to a quantity without converting or checking that both parts use the same unit of measure.

items.stem: Write the fraction 18/24 in simplest form.

options.rationale: 18 and 24 share a common divisor of 6, and 18÷6=3 while 24÷6=4.
Adds 18+24 to make a new numerator and 24+24 to make a new denominator instead of dividing by a common divisor.
Adds the numerator and denominator to replace the numerator, leaving the original denominator.

items.keyRationale: Divide both 18 and 24 by their common divisor 6 to obtain 3/4.

items.stem: What percentage is equivalent to the fraction 3/5?

options.rationale: Writes the digits of the numerator and denominator side by side as a percentage.
Multiplies 3 by 5 and treats the product as a percentage.

rejection.reason: Every incorrect option names a known misconception: 2 distractors have no known misconception: item:au.year-7.mathematics.fraction-decimal-percent-equivalence.01/B, item:au.year-7.mathematics.fraction-decimal-percent-equivalence.01/C. Rejected rather than repaired.

items.stem: On a number line marked from −2 to 3, which value sits exactly halfway between 0 and −1?

options.rationale: The midpoint of 0 and −1 is −0.5, which is −1/2.
Uses the positive halfway mark instead of the negative side.
Goes one and a half units left of zero rather than half a unit.

rejection.reason: Every incorrect option names a known misconception: 2 distractors have no known misconception: item:au.year-7.mathematics.rationals-on-number-line.01/B, item:au.year-7.mathematics.rationals-on-number-line.01/C. Rejected rather than repaired.

items.stem: A bag has red and blue counters in the ratio 2:3. What fraction of all the counters is red?

options.rationale: 2 red parts plus 3 blue parts make 5 equal parts in total, so red is 2/5 of the whole.
Treats the two ratio numbers as unrelated and writes red over blue with no shared whole.
Reads the parts as two separate counts and inverts them without forming a total.

items.keyRationale: The whole is 2+3=5 parts, so red is 2/5.

items.stem: Share $40 in the ratio 2:3. How much does the first share receive?

options.rationale: 2+3=5 parts; each part is $40÷5=$8; first share is 2×$8=$16.
Gives the written ratio numbers as the dollar amounts and ignores scaling to $40.
Assigns the second ratio number as a dollar amount without finding the value of one part.

items.keyRationale: Five equal parts of $8 give a first share of $16.

items.stem: A cordial mix uses 200 mL of syrup to 1 L of water. How many millilitres of water are needed for 100 mL of syrup?

options.rationale: 1 L=1000 mL, so the ratio is 200:1000=1:5. Half the syrup needs half the water, 500 mL.
Uses the ratio numbers 200 and 1 without converting litres to millilitres.
Applies 200:1 directly to 100 mL and drops the unit conversion.

items.keyRationale: Convert 1 L to 1000 mL so both parts use millilitres, then scale 200:1000 to 100:500.
